questions.q: A reader finishes page 30 of a script and the story is still heading in the same direction it started. In Field's terms, what's missing?
choices: A crisis decision between two irreconcilable goods
Plot Point I: an event that spins the action in a new direction
A false victory at the midpoint
A save-the-cat moment for the hero
questions.explain: Field's Plot Point I, around page 25–27, hooks into the action and turns it into Act II.

questions.q: Why can Field attach page numbers to his acts at all?
choices: Because studios require scripts of exactly 120 pages
Because Aristotle specified the proportions
Because one page of screenplay runs about one minute of screen time
Because every act must contain the same number of scenes
questions.explain: The page-a-minute rule of thumb turns page numbers into a rough map of the film.

questions.q: Field says his paradigm is 'context', not 'content'. What does he mean?
choices: It gives the structure that holds a story, not what happens in it
It applies only to the setting of a story
It describes the theme, not the plot
It's meant for adaptations rather than original scripts
questions.explain: The paradigm tells you something must turn the story around page 25. Only the writer can supply what.

questions.q: A writer's sixty-page Act II wanders. What later addition to Field's model is meant to help?
choices: Four-corner opposition
Breaking the film into eight sequences of 10–15 minutes
Moving the climax to the middle of the play
A midpoint around page 60 that splits Act II into two halves
questions.explain: In The Screenwriter's Workbook Field described the midpoint, which gives the second act a turn and two halves.

questions.q: What does Field mean by a character's 'dramatic need'?
choices: A flaw that hurts other people
What the character wants to win, gain, get or achieve over the story
The audience's need to like the hero
The backstory wound that haunts the character
questions.explain: Dramatic need defines the character; drama comes from putting obstacles in its way.

questions.q: Which criticism of Field comes from close timing of real Hollywood films?
choices: That most films break into four roughly equal parts, not a 1–2–1 shape
That every scene must turn a value
That a hero must be likable
That stories should grow organically from a premise
questions.explain: Kristin Thompson's analysis found four balanced parts; Field's own midpoint goes some way toward the same idea.

questions.q: What should a reader know within roughly the first ten pages of a Field-style script?
choices: The ending and the theme
Who the main character is, what the story is about, and the situation
The B story and its love interest
The villain's plan
questions.explain: Field puts heavy weight on the opening: main character, dramatic premise and dramatic situation.

ideas: A plot point is an event that hooks into the action and spins it around in another direction.
A screenplay is a story told with pictures, and one page runs about a minute of screen time.
A feature divides into Setup, Confrontation and Resolution of roughly 30, 60 and 30 pages.
Structure is the context that holds a story; the content is something only the writer can supply.
